title: Data from Configuration Repository
summary: Data from Configuration Repository covers collection aimed at the central systems that hold configuration and management data for many devices at once, rather than at the devices themselves. These repositories are the memory of a management platform: they store device configuration files, software inventories, interface and address details, routing information, and frequently the credentials or keys the platform uses to log in to everything it manages. An adversary who reads from them obtains, in a single movement, a map of the estate, a list of valid service accounts, and the exact build of each device, which directly serves discovery and sets up later targeting. Access usually travels over management protocols such as Simple Network Management Protocol, Smart Install, Trivial File Transfer Protocol, Secure Copy Protocol or a management application programming interface, so it looks like normal administrative traffic unless the source, timing, volume or account is wrong. Detection depends on management plane telemetry: authentication and command logs on the repository and its clients, records of configuration exports and bulk queries, unusual query depth or repeated walks, downloads of many configuration files by one account, and access from hosts that never normally manage the network. The legitimate pattern is a small set of management hosts, scheduled jobs, named automation accounts and predictable volumes; the malicious pattern is off schedule, from unusual sources, and broad rather than targeted.

beginner.definition: A configuration repository is a central store where management software keeps settings and details for many devices. This technique describes an attacker reading that store. They take the information, not the devices.
beginner.whyItMatters: One repository often describes an entire network in one place. It can list device models, addresses and management accounts. Reading it saves an attacker weeks of guessing and can hand over credentials. The theft is quiet, because reading data usually changes nothing. Without management plane logging, you may only learn about it much later.
howItWorks: The attacker first reaches the management network or a management service there.
They query the repository using a normal protocol such as Simple Network Management Protocol.
They pull device details, interface lists and software versions together in bulk.
They may also export full configuration files taken from many devices at once.
Those files often contain account names, shared secrets and detailed network layout.
The attacker now holds a complete map plus credentials for future targeting.
beginner.example: Imagine the back office of a large post office. Every delivery route, every staff locker number and every building key code is written in one ledger there. A thief does not need to break into a hundred houses. He only needs ten quiet minutes with the ledger, and he can photograph every route and key code in the city. Nobody notices, because the ledger is still on the shelf and nothing is missing. A configuration repository is that ledger. Reading it is not a break in, yet it can hand an attacker almost everything needed for the next stage.
takeaways: Configuration repositories hold credentials and layout data, so guard them like a server.
Log every management query and configuration export, and record the account used.
Restrict management protocols to dedicated hosts and networks.

objectives: Describe what a configuration repository stores and why it is valuable to an attacker.
Explain how collection from a repository supports later discovery and targeting.
Identify management plane log sources that record repository access.
Distinguish normal automation traffic from bulk collection.
Explain why reading configuration data is hard to notice without logging.
List the sensitive data types typically found inside configuration files.
